name: Echolalia
summary: Repeating words or phrases heard from someone else — either immediately or after a delay — which is common in autistic communication and often serves a real communicative or self-regulatory function rather than being meaningless repetition.
triggers: Being asked a question that is hard to answer spontaneously
Anxiety or stress, where repeating familiar phrases is soothing
Processing language that is still being learned (a step toward spontaneous speech)
Enjoyment of the sound, rhythm, or memory associated with a phrase
A gap in expressive language for the situation at hand

remedies.text: Treat echolalia as communication and try to interpret its likely function (request, protest, self-soothing) rather than only trying to suppress it
Speech-language therapy individualized to the person, since echolalia responds best to programs tailored to the specific communicative function it serves
Model the target phrase in response rather than correcting — e.g. answering an echoed question with the expected reply, giving a pattern to imitate
Visual supports (picture cards, written scripts) to help build alternative ways to express the same need

sources.label: PMC - Functional echolalia in autism speech: Verbal formulae and repeated prior utterances as communicative and cognitive strategies
